speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of Stale for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: TANGANYIKA
subsubtopic: CANADIAN HIGH COMMISSIONER
speechtext:
Last December, Mr. Speaker, I announced that the government had decided to extend its diplomatic relations with the independent states of Africa by opening new diplomatic missions in Tanganyika and the Federal Republic of Cameroon. I am pleased to announce today that an experienced officer of my department, Mr. Norman Berlis, has been appointed as the first Canadian high commissioner to Dar-es-Salaam, Tanganyika.
This appointment is a mark of the importance which the government attaches to the establishment of close relations between this new member of the commonwealth and Canada. Mr. Berlis, a native of Toronto, is a graduate of the University of Toronto and Osgoode Hall, and has had extensive service for Canada both during the war and in the Department of External Affairs. At present he is head of the information division. The Canadian mission in Dar-es-Salaam will have important functions to fulfil, particularly in the field of educational and technical assistance under the special commonwealth African aid program.
As an example of the close and friendly cooperation between Canada and the former British colonies in Africa, the house might be interested to know that during the visit to Ottawa on December 17 of the chief minister of Uganda, Hon. B. K. W. Kiwanuka, who is the first minister, I discussed with him the ways in which Canada might be able to extend assistance to his country under the special commonwealth aid to Africa program. The proposal to which he gave highest priority was the attachment of a senior foreign service officer to the Canadian delegation to the United Nations in New York.
I am glad to be able to inform the house that we have already acted on this request. Mr. A. K. Kironde, a former Uganda minister of works, who is to become ambassador and head of the Uganda delegation to the United Nations when his country becomes independent on October 9 of this year, has joined our New 26207-1-19
York delegation as an observer as of January 25 after spending three days in Ottawa, and he will continue with the delegation until he becomes permanent representative of Uganda. Canada is paying his expenses from our special commonwealth aid to Africa funds.
The appointment of Mr. Berlis and this request from Uganda that we help to train their permanent representative at the United Nations are very significant moves, because they are the first moves into east Africa; in due course our high commissioner to Tanganyika will probably also be credited to Uganda and to Kenya.

subtopic: FALL-OUT PROTECTION, FEDERAL BUILDINGS
FALL-OUT PROTECTION, FEDERAL BUILDINGS
speechtext:
1.	Since September 13. 1961, how many federal buildings (a) have been considered to have adequate fall-out protection (b) can be improved to provide such protection, and what is the estimated cost of making such improvements and providing essential facilities and supplies (c) cannot be thus improved due to the excessive costs involved?
2.	Are steps being taken to so improve such buildings to provide adequate fall-out protection, and when is it estimated that this work will be completed?
3.	How many of the buildings referred to respectively in (a), (b), and (c) of part 1 of this question are in target cities?
4.	How many of the said buildings were considered to have been destroyed during exercise Tocsin B?
Answer by: Mr. Diefenbaker:
1.	During 1961 surveys of federal buildings with respect to fall-out protection have been carried out by two departments, the Department of Public Works and the Department of National Defence. Since the surveys by the Department of National Defence and the evaluation of them will not be completed until March 31, 1962, the information given here refers to the information gathered by the Department of Public Works only.
In its surveys it has been found that 504 federal buildings are considered to have adequate fall-out protection. In its opinion 324 additional buildings can be altered to provide adequate fall-out protection at an estimated cost of approximately $5,000,000 for the necessary improvements and essential facilities and supplies. Some 4,000 other federally owned buildings could only be provided with fall-out protection at considerably greater cost.
2.	The results of the detailed surveys described in 1 are at present under consideration and no decision to undertake construction has yet been made.
3.	Of the 828 federal buildings, including
the 504 with adequate fall-out protection and the 324 that could economically be modified, there are 281 in areas listed as possible target areas.	.
4.	Of these 828 buildings, it is estimated that 214 would have been destroyed under the circumstances assumed in exercise Tocsin B. No detailed review was made of the other buildings.

subtopic: FALL-OUT PROTECTION FACILITIES, TARGET AREAS
FALL-OUT PROTECTION FACILITIES, TARGET AREAS
speechtext:
Since September 13, 1961, has the emergency measures organization, or any other part of government developed any measures to give priority to target areas for increasing fall-out protection for those dwelling in private houses or apartment houses by making it possible for people to make use of government, privately owned, commercial, and industrial buildings, and, if so, what are those measures?
Questions
Answer by: Mr. Diefenbaker: Since September 13,	1961, the emergency measures
organization, together with other agencies of government immediately concerned, such as the Department of Public Works, has been considering measures, with special attention to target areas, that would increase fall-out protection for those dwelling in private houses or apartment houses, by making it possible for people to use government, privately owned, commercial, and industrial buildings. Before firm recommendations can be made in this matter, it has been found necessary to procure a good deal of basic information. This includes the number of buildings that already have a reasonable degree of protection against radioactive fall-out, what buildings could economically be modified to afford such protection, what numbers of people under emergency conditions they would accommodate, what costs would be involved in improving the fall-out protection factor, and numerous other related facts.
While various buildings of the types enumerated above are subject to consideration, first priority has been given to federally owned buildings. The next group given attention includes those owned by provincial and municipal governments. Extensive surveys have been carried on by the Department of Public Works with respect to federally owned buildings and these surveys are supplemented by those now in progress by the Department of National Defence with respect to army buildings. Concurrently, provinces and municipalities have been encouraged to undertake sur veys of buildings they own. These surveys are now going forward at numerous points in Canada.
The federal government has provided technical advice and in some instances has provided personnel as well to assist in the surveys. The costs of such surveys made by provinces and municipalities are recognized as an appropriate part of the financial assistance program for emergency planning, and thus to the extent of 75 per cent are met from federal funds.
Beyond the buildings owned by various governments it would be anticipated that commercial and industrial buildings would fall into the next priority for survey purposes. When the degree of fall-out protection afforded by such buildings and their capacity for habitation for survival purposes have been determined, then measures for possible use of such buildings in an emergency can be given detailed consideration.

subtopic: NUCLEAR DEVICE EXPLOSION, ATHABASCA TAR SANDS
NUCLEAR DEVICE EXPLOSION, ATHABASCA TAR SANDS
speechtext:
1.	Have any requests been received from, or have any discussions taken place with (a) the governments of Alberta or the United States of America (b) private oil companies, concerning the explosion of a nuclear device in the Athabasca tar sands in Alberta?
2.	If so, on what dates, and what was the federal government's answer in each case?
Answer by: Mr. Churchill: The possibility of recovering oil from Athabasca tar sands by the explosion of a nuclear device was brought to the attention of several federal government organizations by a private oil company in 1958. As a result, the former minister of mines and technical surveys set up a committee to investigate the technical feasibility of this proposal. This committee was composed of technical representatives from the oil company and federal and Alberta government organizations and it had discussions with technical officers of the United States atomic energy commission, who had carried out underground tests in that country.
Though there have been discussions on the technical level regarding the feasibility of such an experiment, there have been no formal discussions with the governments of Alberta or the United States of America regarding the actual carrying out of an explosion in the Alberta tar sands. The Prime Minister advised, in answer to a question on March 21, 1960-Hansard, p. 2251-that the atomic energy control board, which would have to approve such an experiment, had not received any application for permission to carry out any such explosion. This is still the situation.

asked the Prime Minister to consider whether the Canadian government could provide food for these refugees and air transport for its delivery to them.

The Prime Minister replied that the Canadian government was deeply concerned both about the events which led to the flight of the Tibetan refugees and about the trials which the Tibetan people were still undergoing. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska asked the following question:
Is it possible that American farmers, who get subsidies to reduce their grain acreage, may be doing some farming in Canada to take advantage of Canadian legislation?
It is not quite clear what the hon. member means by this question but if he is referring to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act and the western grain producers' acreage payments, I can assure him that only those producers ordinarily or permanently resident in Canada are eligible for assistance.

The house in committee of supply, Mr. Chown in the chair.
DEPARTMENT OF AGRICULTURE Production and marketing branch-
611. Payments to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely, $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $42,000,000.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to participate in the debate on this particular estimate which will provide $1 an acre to western farmers. Those
Supply-Agriculture
of us who are familiar with the situation in the west know that the farmers had a very short crop. We know that many farmers have not been able to deliver beyond their initial quota. We know that many farmers, having reached the three bushel quota, did not have any more grain or, if they did, they retained it for spring. We also know that there were perhaps a small number of farmers who had a little surplus from other years, but this has rapidly dwindled.
I welcome the opportunity to support this item because it will provide something of a two price system. For years many western farmers have been clamouring for this type of measure and for years the Liberal government at Ottawa refused it. I also welcome the opportunity to support this measure because it will assist those who have not been able to qualify for payments under the Prairie Farm Assistance Act for various reasons.
I have one objection, however, in that the measure does not cover landlords. On March 17, 1961, while participating in a debate on agriculture, as found in volume 3 of Hansard for that year at page 3111, I outlined what I thought was the solution to this problem, and if the government will take note of it I think we will have that problem solved. With that one reservation I am in complete support of this measure.
No doubt the opposition will holler "peanuts." The circus barker from Assiniboia has referred to this and similar measures as "peanuts" on many occasions. The same cry was picked up by the provincial minister of agriculture. As found in the Star-Phoenix of December 14 last, Mr. Nollet had this to say after the acreage payments had been announced:
Saskatchewan agriculture minister I. C. Nollet said that "every little bit helps" but described the payments as "peanuts" and said farmers were expecting more than received under similar payments previously in light of the "great crop losses" this year.
This is the minister of agriculture who now calls himself C.C.F.-N.D.P. This is the same minister of agriculture who, when the crop was snowed under in 1959 and there was a clamour for $5 per acre, took up that clamour too. When the federal government said, "All right, if you will pay half", he said, "Oh, no". He said, "Cut it down to $3". In addition he put forward some sort of magic sliding scale under which many farmers received only 20 cents an acre.
This is the same minister who cries "peanuts" today and says that a greater amount should be provided. This is the same C.C.F.-N.D.P. minister of agriculture of our great province of Saskatchewan who, when the federal government introduced crop insurance,

Supply-Agriculture
said "No, it will break the province". That cry went up all over the west, and the hon. member for Assiniboia and the C.C.F.-N.D.P., or whatever they call themselves now, took up that same cry; "it will break the province". At the same time they introduced a medical scheme which is going to cost somewhere in the neighbourhood of $25 million. This is not supposed to break the province because it is supposed to boost Douglas. This is an acreage scheme to repay the farmer for crop losses, whereas the medical scheme was proposed for their own political gain. Why is there such concern that it will break the province? Surely there must be some way, such as reinsurance, to work out to details of this scheme. Why do they show such concern for the state and none for the individual farmer? Since when has the state become more important than the individual? Apparently in the eyes of the socialists the state must be preserved but the individual can suffer.
The hon. member for Assiniboia referred to the program as peanuts and said it would amount to nothing.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: You are wrong again.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext:
I can tell the hon. member what it will do for my constituency. I have checked and I find I have over 6,000 permit books in my constituency. If we take 1960 as an average, this would mean about $186 per book or something like $35,000 for every community. Now, if you take this $35,000 as the average and apply it against the assessment of my own rural municipality of Invermay, assuming an average mill rate of 60 mills, we find that this $35,000 will go a long way toward paying the taxes of the municipality. There are two communities in this municipality. At $35,000 to each community it represents almost all the taxes paid by the taxpayers. I say that this is not peanuts.
The Liberal spokesman, the hon. member for Essex East, had a lot to say about this program. I should like to quote, for example, what he said as recorded on page 263 of Hansard for January 26, 1962:
I repeat that the Prime Minister and his supporters cannot claim that by this particular program they are satisfying the promises which were made to hundreds of Canadian western farmers.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: We are satisfying a very large number of farmers.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext:
I sincerely hope that is the case but, as I have stated, this provision does not meet the objectives of the government's declared farm policy as announced by the Prime Minister. It does not meet the assurances given to a thousand western farmers when they descended on Ottawa two years ago to demand that this government implement its agriculture policy.

This speech by the Liberal spokesman reminds me of a little jingle. What he says does not mean anything or, in the words of the jingle, "I planted corn in early spring but it didn't mean a dog-gone thing; what do you think came up in the fall? The crows came up and ate them all."
I have a list of things here to illustrate how wrong the hon. member for Essex East is. Somewhere along the line the hon. member for Assiniboia intervened and said, "What about the one year you did not pay?" I say to the hon. member for Assiniboia, what was he doing all the years he was in the house?

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, on a point of order-

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: He was a C.C.F. member at the time-

speechtext: On a point of order, Mr. Chairman; a question has been asked as to what I was doing. The answer is that I have been prodding, pushing and pleading with the government to give at least a dollar an acre every year.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: Very well; the hon. member says he has been pushing and prodding and wailing for all these years. I point out, however, that in 1945 there were 28 C.C.F. members in the house; in 1949 there were 13; in 1953, 23; in 1957, 25 and in 1958 after the large group of Conservatives were elected from the west, there were only eight C.C.F. members; but we got our acreage payments.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: Yes, but I have always been here.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: It would appear that the effectiveness of the farm support program is in reverse proportion to the number of socialists in the house.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: The hon. member just wants a one party dictatorship.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext:
I come back to the hon. member for Essex East who at one time sat as a minister on the Liberal front benches. I find that since the introduction of the price stabilization bill and up to March 31, 1961, we have paid out $126 million in support of the farmers across Canada, not for one particular area but for all across Canada. As a matter of fact, the price stabilization measure has been much more effective in the east than in the west, but we are not complaining about that. Under the Liberal regime from 1946 to 1958 there was spent about $100 million. However, about $70 million of that was spent at a time when foot-and-mouth disease was prevalent in the west. In the past few years we have spent something like $126 million, while in

12 years the Liberals spent a grand total of $100 million. However, if it had not been for the catastrophe of foot-and-mouth disease they would have spent only $30 million.
Where was the hon. member for Essex East when the farmers were asking for cash advances?

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: I was working hard for the people of Canada.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: Where was he when they were asking for crop insurance? Where was he, as a member of the opposition, when we introduced the amendments to the Prairie Farm Assistance Act so that 15 per cent more farmers could benefit? Where was he when the farmers, over the years, asked for the South Saskatchewan dam? It only took a very short time for the Conservatives to provide this dam which will be beneficial to the farmers of Saskatchewan and to the west in general.

subtopic: EFFORTS BY UNITED STATES FARMERS TO BENEFIT FROM CANADIAN LAW
speechtext: I rise on a point of order. I would simply recall, Mr. Chairman, to your mind that when the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska spoke the other day and sought to deal with agricultural problems in general he was arrested in his steps by the intervention of the Acting Minister of Agriculture. I am sure if that is to be the ruling, then it ought to apply to members on the government side as well as to those on this side.

speechtext: If I may speak to that point of order, Mr. Chairman, I would say that at page 263 of Hansard for January 26, the hon. member for Essex East said that the Prime Minister and his supporters could not claim this particular program was satisfying the promises which were made to hundreds of Canadian western farmers. against the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska and strictly enforced against me and others who spoke, as a result of the intervention of the Acting Minister of Agriculture. Now, the hon. gentleman is not in a privileged position.

speechtext: If I may speak to this point of order, I would say that at five o'clock on Friday night the hon. member for Essex East was engaged in filibustering this vote. He spoke of nothing but what his leader was going to say, and he broke the rule himself.

Between these two opposing views one has to make a decision. Is agriculture really on a sound economic basis, as indicated by the Prime Minister, or does agriculture in a general way need to be assisted? For my part I have no hesitation in deciding that farmers are not now enjoying prosperous times and need such assistance as is provided by this measure. However, I feel I must emphasize before this committee that the western farmers are not alone in facing financial difficulties at the present time. What is true of the western farmers is in greater measure true of farmers in the eastern regions.
Let me cite two examples. We are all aware that the dairy industry, which is the main source of income for a great number of eastern farmers particularly, is now beset with very serious circumstances. The Canadian dairy association only a short time ago submitted to the government a measure aimed at bringing relief to this situation. All those concerned with this matter are now aware of the government's refusal to accept those recommendations.
Second, the potato industry is also of great concern to eastern farmers and particularly to New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island farmers. These farmers have to sell their 1961 crop at the present time at a price under the cost of production. Here again, where is

The other day, and again just now, the hon. member who preceded me seems to have slipped into that failing. The other day, as I said, the hon. member for Drummond-Arthabaska (Mr. Boulanger), spoke in favour of payments to western wheat producers whose crops were seriously damaged by the drought, but, at the same time, he wondered why the eastern provinces should not benefit in the same way when disaster strikes. What the hon. member has failed to mention is that when such a disaster occurs,

the provincial government is supposed to carry out a survey of the damage and get in touch with the authorities of the Department of Agriculture. Of course, that depends on whether or not the provincial government itself is willing to ask for help of the federal government.

MEASURE TO PROVIDE FOR A NATIONAL FLAG OF CANADA  OFFICIAL NATIONAL ANTHEM
speechtext:
That a special joint committee of both houses of parliament be appointed to consider ways and means of giving Canada a distinctive flag and an official national anthem:
That, notwithstanding standing order 67, the said committee, on the part of this house, shall consist of 25 members, to be named at a later date, and that the quorum shall be as ordered by the said committee;
That the said committee be empowered to hear in this connection the views of Canadian organizations, public bodies and private citizens, to send for persons, papers and records; to sit while the house is sitting; to report from time to time; and to print such papers and evidence from day to day as may be ordered by it and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto; and
That a message be sent to the Senate requesting their honours to unite with this house for the above purpose and, if the Senate deems advisable, to appoint some of its members to act on the said committee.
(Translation):
Mr. Speaker, first of all I should like to read the following motion to the house.
That a special joint committee of both houses of parliament be appointed to consider ways and means of giving Canada a distinctive flag and an official national anthem;
That, notwithstanding standing order 67, the said committee, on the part of this house, shall consist of 25 members to be named at a later date and that the quorum shall be as ordered by the said committee;
That the said committee be empowered to hear, in this connection, the views of Canadian organizations, public bodies and private citizens; to send

Provision for National Flag and Anthem for persons, papers and records; to sit while the house is sitting; to report from time to time; and to print such papers and evidence from day to day, as may be ordered by it and that standing order 66 be suspended in relation thereto; and
That a message be sent to the Senate requesting their honours to unite with the house for the above purpose and, if the Senate deems advisable, to appoint some of its members to act on the said committee.
Mr. Speaker, needless to say that the great majority of Canadians are in favour of a distinctive national flag as well as a national anthem.
It would be interesting, if that motion is agreed upon, if various organizations across the country appeared before this committee; for instance, this committee could call the premiers of the various provinces which comprise the Canadian nation.
It would be interesting to hear Mr. Smallwood's opinion on what he understands to be a "distinctive national flag" as well as Mr. Bennett's, from British Columbia, and that of other premiers.
Mr. Speaker, need I remind you that the Canadian Chamber of Commerce, on many occasions, during its conventions, unanimously passed a motion requesting the adoption of a distinctive national flag.
The Knights of Columbus of Canada have also adopted a similar resolution.
The Catholic and national unions, and particularly those of Joliette, have already submitted to me a brief asking that I request in the house the adoption of a national flag, and of the national anthem "O Canada".
The National Federation of Canadian University Students, at its 25th convention held in Kingston, also adopted a resolution requesting a Canadian national flag and a Canadian national anthem, that is, "O Canada". That resolution was introduced by the students of St. Joseph University of Moncton.
The national federation of university students represents 37 Canadian universities and
50,000	students.
The National Youth Movement, affiliated with the Native Sons of Canada, has also requested the adoption of a Canadian flag, white and red with a green maple leaf, and the song "O Canada" as national anthem in all provinces. I believe that the very great majority of Canadians are in favour of the adoption of an exclusively Canadian flag.
On August 5, 1960, the members of the National Youth Movement made a survey at the intersection of Northcote and Queen streets, in Toronto. Here is the result: 74 per


cent of those questioned want an entirely Canadian flag on which the maple leaf would be the main pattern; 21 per cent want a flag with the Union Jack; 1 per cent want the stars and stripes of the United States; and 4 per cent are undecided.
It is a fact that "O Canada" is being heard more and more in Canadian official ceremonies. We know the precedent established at the time of the royal visit, on July 1, 1959, when "O Canada" was played for the first time on the occasion of the march past on Parliament hill. "O Canada" was also played before the Governor General, Mr. Vanier, while he inspected his personal guard for the first time. It is almost never forgotten now, because protests would be immediate. It is a sign of the times.
"O Canada" is a national anthem.
"O Canada" is a truly national anthem for our country. Its words tell the history of our country, with its vast expanses of lakes, prairies, cities, mountains and farms. Never has this song failed to kindle a burning flame of love and pride for our country. For many newcomers to our shores, "O Canada" will be inspiring and will strengthen that spirit of Canadianism which will make them love their new country.
"God Save the Queen" originated in England in the 18th century, amid partisan strife having nothing to do with Canadian traditions. That hymn is waning in the Canadian west, as all those who listened to the 1958 football finals broadcast were able to realize. Our anthem, "O Canada", with its title and words, is a recognition of Canada as an independent nation, freely and willingly associated with the British commonwealth. It is high time for sleep-walkers in our midst to wake up and accept the facts of 1962.
In 1959, the Canadian institute of public opinion was carrying out a poll among Canadians with regard to the choice of a national anthem. The question was put in this way:
These are the titles of four patriotic songs. According to you, which would be most suitable as our national anthem?
O Canada	 67 per cent
God Save the Queen	 20 per cent
The Maple Leaf	 11 per cent
Rule Britannia	 1 per cent
No answer	 1 per cent
This survey took place in 1959, and I am certain that if it were repeated in 1962, the 1959 choice would certainly carry more than 90 per cent of the votes.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) ask for a distinctive national flag. First of all, it would be interesting to know what he means by distinctive, because the Liberals themselves are much divided on that point.
As a matter of fact, there is no need to recall what happened at a certain convention of the Young Liberal Federation of Canada. Referring to Le Devoir of September 28, 1959, I might say that the young Liberals of Canada were divided. I shall now quote that paper:
A Winnipeg delegate, Mr. Allan Barry, said that those who are opposed to the fleur-de-lis and to the union jack have no great Canadian feeling. Those who stand for a positive Canadianism are broadminded enough to recognize the contribution made by France and England to the development of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, need I remind you that order in council 5888 was adopted on Wednesday, September 5, 1945, by the former government. Let me read you a few extracts:
It is desirable to authorize the flying of the Canadian red ensign on federal government buildings and to remove any doubt as to the propriety of flying the Canadian red ensign wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
Therefore, His Excellency the Governor General in council, on the recommendation of the Prime Minister, is pleased to order and doth hereby order that the red ensign with the shield of the coat of arms of Canada in the fly may be flown from buildings owned or occupied by the federal government within and without Canada.
His Excellency in council, on the same recommendation, is further pleased to declare and doth hereby declare that it shall be appropriate to fly the Canadian red ensign within and without Canada wherever place or occasion may make it desirable to fly a distinctive Canadian flag.
Mr. Speaker, that order in council was issued in 1945 under Mackenzie King's government. Who was a member of the cabinet at that time? None other than the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier) who, in 1945, could easily have got up and asked that a truly distinctive flag be adopted contrary to the above-mentioned order in council. The hon. member for Laurier is not the same man today, he is altogether different. Does that mean that he has changed his mind since he has become a member of the opposition?
Must I also remind you of the article which appeared in the newspaper Le Devoir on March 7, 1958? That article was written after the election campaign of 1958 at a time when Mr. Pearson was going from one end of the country to the other, saying one thing in the English speaking provinces and another in Quebec.

Mr. Speaker, I was greatly interested in the speech by the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Argue). I have heard the same speech, of course, on many other occasions when a private bill has been debated in the house. It is typical of the tactics he employs to take the opportunity and use part of the available time for purely political purposes. He informs the house how serious such a measure as this is, how important it is to the country as a whole that the measure be passed, what rascals we all are if we dare to talk about the subject, and then tells us we should vote on it quickly once he has made his usual political speech. I am not one of those who believe that this speech the hon. member makes is going to fool anyone in the country. If he would recognize that the people of this country who are adult enough to appreciate a flag or a national anthem are adult enough to be wise to this sort of tactic, especially after it has been used this length of time, the hon. member would not waste so much time. However, I do not want to fall into the hon. member's habit and talk only about the political aspects of the measure before us.
I believe that a lot of serious consideration must be given to the question of a flag or a national anthem, and much serious consideration must be given to the manner in which a flag shall be chosen. I suggest that when we are considering the question of whether or not this country should have a distinctive 26207-1-22
flag, we should reflect for a while on some of the more important uses of that flag. Certainly, those of us who have been in a foreign country, especially if you have difficulty speaking the language or you run a little short of money and do not know where there is a bank or where to turn for help, know how advantageous it is to spot a flag that is a distinctive symbol of home. I would suggest that one of the most important uses of the flag is to mark a little bit of Canadian soil, a friend from Canada, whether it is a ship or anything else. It is a way of letting it be known that here is a Canadian, here is a little bit of Canada or someone who is a friend of Canada's.
Many people, of course, would like to have a flag flying in their own home as a daily reminder of their Canadian citizenship. Many people would like to have the flag in the classroom or would like to start classes by the singing of the national anthem as a sort of reminder that we are an independent, sovereign nation. Certainly, the fact that Canada is not a colony cannot be emphasized too strongly in some parts of the world; we are a free, independent and sovereign nation.
If we had our own flag it would serve as a reminder that Canada is a distinct entity. I should like to caution some of those members who are most worried about the subject that there is more than the spirit of nationalism to be considered. Certainly, we are all proud of being Canadians and we would like to display some symbol to show our national unity, our national sovereignty. However, it is a question right now of just what that symbol should be and how we should arrive at it. I am suggesting that there are more important considerations to be borne in mind. Canada is growing in stature and has always been a most complex nation in terms of national background and the heritage of the people who make up this country. The flag has the purpose of drawing us together, to help give us national unity, to help make us a national entity. I suggest, Mr. Speaker, it is most difficult at this stage of the development and growth of this country to clearly define that national entity.
If it is as difficult to define a Canadian as I feel it is, then how much more complex and difficult is it to find a symbol that will show to the world what "Canadian" means, a symbol that will satisfy all people in this country, or at least the vast majority of them?
I suggest that being a true Canadian, a distinctive Canadian, means at least a dozen different things in our country at the present time. There is one large group, the French Canadian group, which feels that the true Canadian spirit is the spirit of the French

tomary to refer to decisions of other courts throughout the commonwealth, and indeed quite often to cases in the British empire. Now, in dealing with the heritage we have gained from Great Britain I might seem to be someone from England, but, on reflection, I am sure my friends realize my surname is Irish and the heritage I get from the Irish through my father is not such that all things British are particularly precious to me.
