611. Payments to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely, $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council, $42,000,000.

It being six o'clock I do now leave the chair.
At six o'clock the committee took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The committee resumed at 8 p.m.

Mr. Chairman, when this debate was interrupted at five o'clock in order to proceed to other business, I had almost concluded my remarks. I had already expressed my support for the measure before the committee and indicated that I felt that acreage

payments had the support of the farmers as well as the business people in the constituency I represent.
I was pointing out the attitude adopted by opposition spokesmen; how they bitterly criticized these payments to western grain producers and then concluded by saying that acreage payments would be of benefit and that they would support the measure. We are accustomed to seeing hon. members of the opposition throw up smokescreens of this type. The former leader of the C.C.F., now the house leader of the C.C.F.-New Democratic party, engaged in a great verbal barrage in finding fault with the agricultural policy of the government in general and concluded by saying that the measure would have his support.
I commend the government for taking this action. I also wish to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture. I am sorry that he is absent due to illness. I wish him a speedy recovery and a quick return to his place in this house.
In concluding I express the hope that the estimates before us will be passed quickly so that cheques can go forward to the farmers of the prairie provinces.

Mr. Chairman, I have just a few brief remarks to make in the light of some of the discussion that has already taken place. Before proceeding with my remarks I wish to join with those hon. members who have already spoken in expressing regret that the Minister of Agriculture is indisposed and unable to be with us at this time to discuss a very important estimate of his department. The minister was extremely kind to the members of the party that went west some days ago to attend the funeral of the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner. Undoubtedly the severe weather in Saskatchewan at that time contributed to the minister's catching 'flu. I wish him a speedy recovery and a rapid return to his place in this house. I am sure hon. members understand that while in debate we are sometimes very sharp and critical one with the other, our good wishes go forward to any hon. member or friend who happens to be ill. May I say for the record that I greatly appreciate the telegram sent to me from the office of the Minister of Agriculture on his behalf and on behalf of his assistant wishing me a speedy recovery when I sustained a slight illness last fall.
We are discussing an estimate to provide for the payment of $1 an acre to western farmers up to a maximum of 200 acres. A number of reasons have been put forward concerning why this item has been brought before us. When it was first discussed in this
Supply-Agriculture
chamber in August of 1958 the original rationale of the Prime Minister was that the payment was in lieu of a two-price system. It was explained that a step was being taken through which the people of Canada would make a contribution to western grain producers who, in the opinion of the government and hon. members generally, were not receiving an adequate price for wheat and certainly not for that going into domestic consumption.
Our position in relation to this item has been clear from the beginning. We feel the farm organizations were correct in asking the government for deficiency payments on wheat, oats and barley, to compensate for the effects of the cost-price squeeze, for the fact that since the end of the war the costs of production of the agricultural industry have increased alarmingly, while the prices of grain in general have increased only slightly if at all.
At the time of the initial announcement of these payments I was highly critical of the government. I said the government did not go far enough in offering this assistance. I am critical again tonight. I do not feel that this present measure is adequate. I feel the government is not keeping faith with the western producers in introducing this item at this time.
I wish to make my position clear. My opinion in this regard has not changed. On August 30, 1958 as reported at page 4351 of Hansard, I had this to say, in part:
This is not a permanent policy, this $40 million item in the estimates. We would naturally welcome any continuation of this as a permanent policy-
Approximately two years later the government announced the payment of $1 an acre once again, making it applicable to a previous period. Today, a year and a half after that, the government is again announcing the payment of $1 an acre, but this is to apply to the present term. The government has skipped a year. We thought this government had a policy. We thought at least the policy meant a dollar an acre, a total item of $40 million a year, in order to compensate for the low price for wheat going into domestic consumption. However, the government has missed a year. This is not a permanent policy; it is a hit or miss policy. When the Prime Minister announced in Prince Albert on December 12 that payments will be recommended, Rudolf Usick, president of the Manitoba farmers union made a statement which reads in part as follows:
The net effect will be that farmers will have missed a whole year's payment because the Prime Minister has not made up his mind on the basis of payment. All farmers need the payments, but they don't appreciate the Prime Minister changing the

Supply-Agriculture
basis of payments again on this hopscotch deal. It means the government has not made a final decision that farmers are entitled to an annual payment.
I suppose even a leader of a farm organization should be careful of his language owing to the supersensitivity of this government. As long ago as 1958, I called this thing "peanuts", in relation to the farmers' costs. Then a strange revelation was made in this House of Commons by the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. He told us why the government missed a year. As found at page 265 of Hansard he said this:
The reason we did not pay it last year was because you shouted "peanuts" and we had a great job trying to sell it again to the government.
I shouted "peanuts" in 1958. I guess the Prime Minister did not quite hear it because in 1960 he paid it again. But apparently in 1961, this single word that was used in 1958 suddenly hit the government and terrified them and they could not bring forward an estimate then because somebody had called out "peanuts". However, they bring it forward today. This is really a bit far fetched, Mr. Chairman, from a group of members who assert that they are getting everything for the farmer when they are speaking in this house. However, I would ask them-and I should like to hear them all do it-to stand up in this debate and call upon the Prime Minister to make a payment in addition to this one for the year that has been missed. This is what the farmers want to know in western Canada. Is this huge number of Tories from the prairies going to say to the Prime Minister, "We want this legislation made permanent; we want this payment for the year that you have missed"? According to his own words the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre is not timid and he knows what he wants. As found on the same page of Hansard to which I referred previously he stated:
When I left home to attend this session of parliament I promised farming groups that I would press for early action in regard to acreage payments. They had asked me to do this.
More than a month earlier the Prime Minister had said he was going to do it. Apparently the hon. member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre did not know about it.
I said "early payment".

Oh, he thought that the Prime Minister would do it but that he might wait too long. You will observe the determination of this man, Mr. Chairman. The Prime Minister says, "I will recommend it to parliament" and the hon. member told the farmers when he left home that he would press for early action with regard to acreage payments.
We get results.

Is the hon. member in favour of paying it for the year that has been missed? That is what I should like to know. Let him stand up and in a clear voice tell the producers of western Canada that he is not only in favour of payment for the present year but that he is in favour of the Prime Minister recommending a payment for the year that has been missed.
We know what hon. members on the other side of the house think of themselves, Mr. Chairman. According to his own words the hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale thinks that you must be on the government side of the house or you are useless. That is what he said. He said that the former hon. member for Peace River, Mr. Solon Low, had been in the house for twenty years and had never got anywhere, and that all he did was to whine.
What are you doing?

That is not right. The former hon. member for Peace River, with whom I disagreed on a great many occasions represented the people of his constituency in a faithful and conscientious manner in my opinion; and I think it ill behooves any member of the House of Commons to say of a man who has served this nation in parliament for 20 years that he was able to get nothing and that all he did when he was here was to whine. We have a distinguished member of this House of Commons who sat on the opposition side for a long time. The hon. member for Prince Albert sat in the opposition for a long time. He whined. He was probably the loudest whiner in the opposition. He whined day after day. He took the hide off the government time after time. He was a good member of the opposition. I think the Prime Minister was an effective member in the opposition.
And he will be again.
Self-delusion.

I think it ill behooves hon. members opposite to try to paint a picture indicating that if you sit on the right of the Speaker and are a Tory, you can get everything done. Who knows, Mr. Chairman, but that the hon. member for Prince Albert might once again in the near future sit on this side of the chamber when he would be obliged to revert to whining again from a bench on the opposition side. The hon. member for Humboldt-Melfort-Tisdale apparently is not satisfied that there are 47 Tories in the 48 ridings in the three provinces. He apparently wants a one party state.
Ask the people of Saskatchewan?

He wants them all of one political stripe. I may tell him that I am pleased that in our best democratic system we not only have a government but an opposition and I hope we shall always have a good and effective opposition in this House of Commons.
That is what the people of Saskatchewan did.

We should like to know from these self-appointed champions what they think about the year that was missed. Let us double the estimates. Let us not have the Prime Minister face an electorate who will say, "You are inconsistent; you gave us valid reasons in 1958 for payment and you gave us valid reasons to make a payment for 1959. What is wrong with a payment for 1961? What happened?" Mr. Chairman, only one thing has happened, apparently, and that is the government's getting closer to an election. Hence they are going to pay it but they are not going to make it permanent by presenting legislation to the House of Commons. They are going to do it by an item in the estimates.
Before the election.

I ask the government, I ask the Acting Minister of Agriculture why he does not recommend to the House of Commons legislation to place this provision in the statute books. By so doing he would save the Prime Minister a great deal of embarrassment. A great many people are going to think this is a payment for an election that is about to come up from a Prime Minister who is so inconsistent that he will not bring forward an item to pay the producers for a year ago. I suggest that the government can be accused of inconsistency. I suggest that the government can be accused of doing this for political purposes.
The people are not as cynical as is the hon. member.

The government has a way- an honourable one, and one in keeping with parliamentary democracy-in which to do this, namely to have the item placed in legislative form. How often has the Prime Minister from this side of the chamber said to the former government that they should not try to legislate through items in the estimates. How often has he said that the way to treat parliament is to bring in legislation, place it on the statute books. Give the people of western Canada a feeling of real confidence that there will be legislation on the statute books and that the moneys will be forthcoming.
I challenge the government to do two things. First, I challenge them to recommend
Supply-Agriculture
payment for the year that has been missed. Second, I challenge the government to bring in legislation. Then they can boast about consistency; then they can boast about a policy of greater permanency. They have overlooked the producers; and the government's 47 members from the west are silent on the question of the year that has been missed. We would like to hear from them as well as from the Acting Minister of Agriculture.

Mr. Chairman, in rising to speak on this particular item of the estimates I think I should first of all say something about the need for it. In the last year western Canada has gone through an exceptionally dry period. Some may not realize, and I know it is hard to do so, just how dry it can get. In western Canada we experienced some dry years in earlier periods and the last year compares well with them. In fact, many oldtimers in the area say that the last year was the driest they ever experienced.
In my particular part of the country there was no grain whatsoever and very little hay, and a lot of feed had to be shipped in to feed the cattle. Just to give hon. members an idea of how dry it was, the farmers in my particular region were cutting hay with diskers. That may be hard to realize but it is a fact. That is how short the crop was. I point this out, Mr. Chairman, only to indicate to hon. members that there is certainly a need for these acreage payments.
Western Canada suffered not only a feed shortage but also a water shortage. Manitoba and Saskatchewan brought into operation water pumping facilities to pump water to livestock. Alberta went so far as to implement a water pumping scheme but only to pump water to towns. Under the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act facilities were provided in order to fill up dugouts that had been dry for the past three years. Western Canada faced a very difficult year, one which would have been much worse if it had not been for the devaluation of the dollar by the government.
We all know that last year there was a great deal of worry about the cattle market because trucks loaded with cattle were lined up going into Winnipeg. Some members felt that there might be a glut of cattle on the market and prices would go down. One can look at the export statistics and see that as soon as the dollar was devalued our cattle started to move across the line to the United States. This not only saved the livestock producers of western Canada but it did a lot for Ontario and Quebec farmers. After all, I come from the province of Alberta which is widely known to have great numbers of cattle

Supply-Agriculture
but it is second among the provinces in that regard. The government stepped in at a crucial time, devalued the dollar and helped the livestock producers to get out of this difficulty. To a great extent the government rescued the mixed farmers of western Canada.
There was also a condition which created a scarcity of feed. At one time Saskatchewan farmers came into the irrigated areas of Alberta and forced the price of hay up to $30 a ton. This happened because of the demand for hay and the fear that there was not going to be any hay to bale. The Alberta and Saskatchewan governments accepted the federal minister's proposal with regard to freight assistance on feed. It was realized that feed could be shipped into these dry areas and sold for less than $30 a ton.
This action in effect put a ceiling on the price of hay. Hay was available in the northern areas of Alberta and the irrigated areas of southern Alberta and could be moved to the buyers at a very small cost. This action went a great way towards saving the livestock industry.
I have no hesitation in supporting this item now before us. I think it will fill to some extent the gap that perhaps has not been covered fully by the other measures to which I have referred, the devaluation of the dollar, the water pumping facilities and the freight assistance on feed.
Western Canada, as I said, faced a difficult year and came through it in relatively good condition. The optimism in western Canada is high today. Why is this so after facing such a difficult year? Because the people of western Canada realize that all through the difficult months of last summer the Minister of Agriculture was on his toes prepared to help and demonstrated to the full his preparedness to help in a difficult time. The minister was not idle abroad. He went out and sought and found markets and convinced the cabinet that these markets should be filled even if we had to sell the grain on credit. This is a very important point because for years farmers and farm groups in western Canada have been asking the federal government to sell a little more grain on credit.
The late Jimmy Gardiner was mentioned, the former minister of agriculture. Although he was an ardent fighter for western Canada, he never did gain the support in cabinet of the hon. member for Essex East. If the hon. member for Essex East had been as ardent a spokesman for the farmers at that time as he is today, he would have given the late minister some help in convincing the former government that some grain should be sold on credit.
In the last year alone approximately $100 million worth of grain has been sold on credit.

This will give hon. members some idea of what this means to the farmers of western Canada and certainly they are grateful for it. They realize that they had a dry year with poor crops in 1961 but were able to sell whatever grain they could harvest and grain they had carried over from previous years. The fact that they were able to sell the grain they had carried over gave them a cash income that they would not have realized if we had not had a minister of agriculture who went out and sold grain and convinced the cabinet that Canada should sell grain on credit. The minister put forward a tremendous effort and moved this grain. This has done a great deal to help to improve the mood of the people of western Canada as they face another year with the hope that there will be more snow this winter and more rain and that things will more or less return to normal.
For the first time since 1952 quotas have been removed. A few years ago those same farmers who could grow nothing this year were realizing that surpluses were their biggest headache. They were afraid of a surplus in cattle. The hon. member for Assiniboia tried to convince us that if we forced the farmers into more livestock production there would be a surplus of cattle. This was the kind of talk that built up fear amongst the farmers in western Canada. Today, we have a Minister of Agriculture who has proven he can sell wheat. We have the markets. We have proven that we can get cattle into the United States market because we have a government that will act. We have captured the faith of the people in western Canada. They know that we are behind them and that their plight is not going unnoticed.
Now, these are very important considerations because I come from a part of the country which is known as the "next year country". When you felt no one was aware of the situation in this part of the country you looked forward to the next year with a certain amount of reluctance, a certain amount of hesitancy in so far as planting a crop is concerned. I can say, Mr. Chairman, that the farmers generally are prepared to go ahead. For the first time since 1952, they realize that they can sell grain if they can grow it. The Minister of Agriculture has told them to produce more livestock if they can, and they are prepared to do so. I was pleased to hear the hon. member for Welland say the other night that he supported this measure. I was pleased to hear that because last Friday afternoon I listened to the hon. member for Essex East and I could not determine whether he was for it or against it. I listened to him all afternoon. He had a difficult time expressing himself about farm

problems, but I must congratulate him because he was probably doing the best he could at the time.
Today and on Friday, Mr. Chairman, we heard very little comment on the deficiency payment scheme which was blasted at us in the house in 1958. Those who spoke skipped over it rather lightly. I think it has been proven that this present measure affords the most farmers some help from the federal government. I believe most people, even the hon. member for Assiniboia, is convinced of this fact. They realize that in a dry year such as western Canada experienced last year the farmers would not receive too much under the deficiency payment plan referred to by a great many people in 1958.
I realize that in 1958 a lot of people were convinced that perhaps the farm unions had something useful in this deficiency payment program, but the government wanted to make sure they were doing the right thing. This might have been some reason for not carrying out the plan in 1959. Certainly, in 1960 it was clearly stated that this scheme was similar to paying a dollar per bushel for wheat consumed in Canada. All the members of this house know the extent to which the farmers of western Canada lost during those years in which our wheat sold below the world price.
The last time these acreage payments were made there was some difficulty experienced because they were made on the permit book for the year previous. I recall that the hon. member for Essex East had a great deal of difficulty understanding the permit book set-up when we debated this matter last year. I happened to have a permit book in my office, so I showed it to him after the debate and I am sure the hon. gentleman was greatly enlightened. Many of the farmers had crops snowed under in 1959, so they did not take out a permit book that year. When the acreage payments were based on these permit books, a lot of farmers experienced a difficult time in obtaining a permit book in order to collect these payments. While we may have missed a year, we are bringing the program up to date. Anyone who has not taken out a permit book this particular year can apply for one, sell some grain if he is fortunate enough to have any, and collect the acreage payment.
This program is designed to help the small farmer who may have been hesitant about taking out a permit book in the previous year but who is entitled to one. I believe this is a good way of doing it. The hon. member for Assiniboia has pointed out that this government has been inconsistent. I have tried, Mr. Chairman, to point out where it
Supply-Agriculture
has been consistent in helping the farmer, in recognizing the situation of the farmer in western Canada. If the hon. member feels the government has been inconsistent in making acreage payments, then he has only himself -to blame because he strongly attacked this policy. Today, we find him in favour of this policy but demanding more money. At times on Friday I thought the hon. member for Essex East wanted more money. However, it seems he did not know whether to go ahead or to go back. He was something like a balky horse, making one plunge ahead and then jumping back. A team of horses pulling that way will never move a load very far.
I should like to point out that you cannot demand a balanced budget, as some members of the official opposition have been doing, and still ask for larger and larger payments under this program. Even the hon. member for Assiniboia was demanding a budget the other day, and I suppose if one had been introduced he would have wanted it balanced. He would have been trying to have his cake and eat it too.
There is just one other point I should like to put on the record and that is with regard to credit assistance in western Canada. I should like to compliment the minister for revamping the Farm Credit Corporation. I should like to advise other members through you, Mr. Chairman, that this program has worked to the tremendous advantage of the small farmers in Saskatchewan, and particularly in Alberta. I have every confidence that this program will continue to serve these farmers in western Canada, and throughout the whole of Canada for that matter. There has been some talk about the rest of Canada being left out of federal assistance. I should like to point out to those members who feel that way that western Canada exports very little butter. Ontario and Quebec receive most of the assistance from the butter support program which represents the other large subsidy being paid by the federal government.
In addition there are those members who feel this support was wrong. The hon. member for Leeds spoke at great length about this the other day, by suggesting that, but he is only hurting the farmers for whom he speaks. We have placed added revenue in the pockets of the farmers by our support of butter prices. I think I have taken up enough time on this particular item and I thank you, Mr. Chairman.

On rising to take part in this discussion. I should like to join with other members who have expressed their regret at

Supply-Agriculture
the fact that illness has prevented the Minister of Agriculture from being in his place during the debate.
We all, of course, wish him a very speedy and complete recovery. Perhaps I might also take advantage of this opportunity to thank the minister for his kindness and his courtesy on the sad occasion of the death of our colleague, Mr. Gardiner, in Saskatchewan, by making transport available for some of us on this side of the house to attend the funeral. As the hon. member for Assiniboia pointed out, it was on that occasion the minister contracted the chill which has kept him indisposed since that particular day. We appreciate all he did on that occasion. We have criticized the minister in this house for some of the policies he has adopted. We are criticizing him today and we shall criticize him in the future but, we acknowledge his characteristic kindness on that occasion.
I venture to say a few words on this item because, among other reasons, there was some reference last Friday to the fact that I had not participated in this debate of such importance to western agriculture and, indeed, that I had not said anything about agriculture in my address on the reply to the speech from the throne. I certainly would not want to disappoint hon. gentlemen opposite, and especially I would not want to disappoint my hon. friend from Essex East who gave the committee an assurance that I would participate. He also gave me some good verbal advice as to what I might say.
Oh, no.

It is very interesting to note, Mr. Chairman, that when it was suggested opposite I should participate in a debate on agriculture the scope of that debate-and I am not complaining about it-was at once limited by your decision to the particular item of acreage payments. For that reason it is very difficult, under the terms of your ruling, to deal with the speech from the throne and with agricultural policies that might have been based on it.
Perhaps I might be permitted to say that when I did take part in that debate I remarked that agriculture was dealt with in a very cursory way and that we intended to deal with other facets of the subject as the debates proceeded in this session. I now have the opportunity to deal with one aspect of agriculture, acreage payments. I would point out, however, that in the debate on the speech from the throne I dealt at some length with one matter which is of the greatest possible importance to agriculture, that is, the widening of our trade opportunities and the removal of obstructions to trade in face of
developments occurring in Europe and other parts of the world. Nothing could be more important to the western farmers and Canadian agriculture generally.
My hon. friend from Acadia, who has just preceded me, in the course of his interesting observations expressed the view that it was difficult to follow the position of the official opposition in their attitude towards this particular item in the estimates. He also said that the hon. member for Essex East spoke about this matter in such a way that it was difficult to find out whether he and the party for which I am now speaking were in favour of the item. He could not have been listening very carefully because if he reads page 261 of Hansard for January 26, 1962 he will find that the hon. member for Essex East said, "We give support to this measure." Surely that is clear enough.
He must have clouded the issue as he went along.

I am on my feet at the moment to confirm that particular declaration of support. We presume that this item in the estimates, and I should point out we are proceeding with this matter by an item in the estimates and not by legislation, though it is very difficult to find evidence to support the presumption, is designed to carry out the sentence in the speech from the throne which reads:
The drought in the prairie provinces during 1961 has resulted in severe losses, however, and you will be asked to provide assistance by means of acreage payments to the farmers who have been affected.
It is perfectly clear, as has been pointed out by some other speakers from this side of the house, that this is not an item designed to carry out the pledge in the speech from the throne. This is an acreage payment item for income maintenance without any specific relevance to drought conditions. If this is the only measure to be brought forth by the government to deal with that proposal in the speech from the throne, then it is completely inadequate for the purpose and, indeed, is not specifically designed for that purpose at all. I do not think it will deceive farmers who have suffered from drought, for the reasons I have just mentioned.
It will of course, be welcomed by those farmers who qualify to receive it but it has nothing to do with the drought as a special, and in places, a tragic situation for certain western farmers. The reason for that is obvious. It has been pointed out by other speakers that this acreage payment will be paid, on exactly the same basis, to all farmers who qualify, whether on the acreage in question they produced no wheat, or whether they produced an above average crop of wheat on

their particular 200 acres, whether they produced wheat for sale and tried to sell it, or whether they produced wheat for feed and did not try to sell it.
To describe this particular proposal, which is one of income maintenance applying to all farmers who qualify, as a drought relief measure such as is described in the speech from the throne, is to say the least misrepresentation.
I believe it has been pointed out by some speakers that those farmers who particularly suffered from drought, and who need special assistance, would get that assistance under a piece of Liberal legislation known as P.F.A.A. I would ask the Acting Minister of Agriculture when he winds up this discussion to tell me if I am not correct-and if I am not correct, I am sure he will tell me- whether there has not been a greater amount of money given to farmers on storage payments under legislation introduced by the previous government than has been paid out to farmers on these acreage payment items in the estimates.
We have another criticism of this measure. This has already been made by speakers on this side of the chamber and I am not going to spend very much time repeating it. We criticize this measure because it is not a cure, it is a palliative. It is not based on* any principle which could be applied to all producers in the future who operate under the same conditions. It is an expedient; it is ad hoc legislation brought in by the government at a particular time when the government may desire to do it-and at this particular time they are doing it on the eve of an election.
It certainly does not begin to carry out the principles and the policies so often laid down by the Prime Minister for parity, not charity and for the necessity of doing something to meet the cost-price squeeze.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, what alternative does the hon. gentleman suggest?
When the time comes we will have some very good suggestions to make, and-

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: When?

-on which to base agricultural policy; not on ad hoc expedients but on principles of general application.
Som hon. Members: Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
speechtext: Would the hon. gentleman tell us tonight what they are?
Mr. Chairman,-

The secret weapon.
Supply-Agriculture

Mr. Chairman, there are
also circumstances attending the introduction of this item in the estimates-this has also been pointed out-that are unusual to say the least. We all recall that when the Minister of Agriculture was out west last November he expressed regret that it would not be possible to make any acreage payments to farmers during the year 1961. He did not base that regret on solid, constitutional reasons, that the item had not been passed, that parliament had not been asked to deal with it. That would have been, if not a satisfactory explanation, a very complete one. He based the reason for the delay in payment on the fact that the cheque-writing machines were overworked and they were busy on other duties at the time. Therefore any payment to be made would have to be made in the new year.
The reason, of course, why he postponed giving anything but a negative announcement on this occasion was that this was to be left to the Prime Minister who, when he was out west on December 13, made the announcement himself in Prince Albert that somehow or other the cheque-writing machines would be all in action again at the beginning of the year, that the House of Commons would be asked to pass this estimate and it would be made available then for those farmers who qualified for it.
There is another very interesting aspect to the background of this legislation. The Minister of Agriculture, in dealing with the reduction of our surplus grains-and we are all very glad to see those surpluses reduced, Mr. Chairman-said the conclusion could be drawn from the fact that our surplus had been so reduced that it might be unwarranted to increase acreage for wheat in the coming wheat. As evidence of the fallibility of human judgment it was only about a year ago when the Minister of Agriculture was going around the west pleading for farmers to increase their acreage of wheat, and indeed the Acting Minister of Agriculture made the same suggestion when he spoke on this matter last Friday.
I did nothing of the kind.
Mr. Chairman, I expected the minister to say that, so I had better read him back his reference.
Yes, read it back.

This is on page 245 of Hansard. Let us just recall the background for a moment, the statement of the Minister of Agriculture warning farmers against increasing their wheat acreage because the surplus had been reduced and if there happened unfortunately to be another bad year

Supply-Agriculture
this year-a drought, for instance-it might be difficult to meet all the commitments which were coming up. That perhaps was a very desirable warning. But in the face of that the Acting Minister of Agriculture said on January 26, at page 245 of Hansard:
Nevertheless a system of assistance which would considerably encourage the production of certain of these grains and cause a move away from a more diversified type of agriculture in western Canada would be a step in the wrong direction.
That is correct.

So the ministers had better get together on this. The acting minister had better get together with himself. The hon. member for Acadia who has just resumed his seat has something to say about the fact that the previous government had never taken any steps to sell grain on credit abroad. The hon. member was not here at the time, or perhaps he would remember-some of my hon. friends on the front bench should remember-that there was a grain agreement made with the Soviet union a good many years back.
How many million bushels?
It was a very good agreement, under which we sold grain to the Soviet union on credit, more grain on credit than is being sold now under the revised agreement.
Would the hon. member permit a question?
We also had credit agreements with Poland, and I think with Czechoslovakia.
A point of order.
He is too chicken to permit a question.
I thought the Liberals had the answer.
You know how badly the answer would show you up.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member does not seem very aware of the facts of this situation. Hon. members may also recall that grain was disposed of before the present government came into office under counterpart arrangements under the Colombo plan treaty. Therefore to say that no arrangements had been made by the previous government to extend credit to the purchase of grain is completely wrong, to say the least.

I did not say you
never sold any grain. I said you never sold any amount of grain on credit.
Sit down.
The hon. member will have the opportunity of reading his own speech of this evening in Hansard and he will see that I am correct.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: He would not understand it anyhow.

The hon. member, having raised this question of trade agreements under which grain has been sold, may also be interested to know-there has been so much misrepresentation on this question that I should refer to it, Mr. Chairman, as he and other hon. members have raised it-that it was many years ago that we on this side of the chamber took the stand that anything that could be done to sell our surplus food commodities to any country of the world would be a desirable policy. I have before me clippings going as far back as-
Mr. Lamontagne never put the answer in your speech. That is my trump card.
I did not interrupt my hon. friend, and perhaps he will sit down quietly.
Order.
The secret weapon.
Order for the government members also.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Would hon. members allow the Leader of the Opposition, who has the floor, to continue.
It is about time.
I was about to say before I was interrupted by my hon. friend opposite, who was allowed to speak without interruption, a courtesy which is not always extended to us on this side of the chamber-
Hear, hear.

-that these statements have misrepresented and distorted our position, which has been the position on this side over the years, that anything that can be done to dispose of our food surpluses to any country in the world, irrespective of its government, is a good thing to do. Any statement to the contrary distorts, misrepresents and denies the policies we have adopted consistently. This can be proved from the record-
Would the hon. member permit a question?
Why, of course.

The hon. gentleman said that the position of the Liberal party was that anything that could be done would be done to dispose of food surpluses. Why did

the Liberal government not take action to remove the embargo placed on cattle going into the United States before 1947?
Mr. Chairman, I am speaking about grain surpluses and now the hon. member-
The hon. member said food surpluses.
The hon. member now rises-
The hon. gentleman referred to food surpluses.
Sit down.

The hon. member for Acadia who seems a little disturbed at the moment now rises and asks me why I did not do something about the cattle embargo in 1947 at a time when I did not have the honour of being in the government.
I wish to clear up one point-and I have lots of evidence to support it-in the hope that this will be the end of these misrepresentative statements that emanate from the other side of the house in respect to our attitude toward the sales of surplus food to any country in the world to which we can sell this food. Of course we are delighted when our wheat, barley and food products generally find their way into any market of the world, communist China or any other market of the world-
Oh, oh.

The other day it was
said to be treason.

Mr. Chairman, it is extremely difficult to proceed with these continual interruptions which Mr. Disraeli once referred to as the harebrained chatter of irresponsible frivolity.
In view of the fact that the debate has ranged so far and wide on this matter I thought this would be an excellent opportunity to clear up this question once and for all. It is a fine thing to see our wheat surpluses going into the markets of the world It is, of course, a cause for some preoccupation when we lose our traditional markets, when they are diminished. We cannot always count on starvation in communist countries to take care of our surpluses and that is why we have been fortunately able to move those surpluses into those countries at this time.
If my friend the hon. member for Acadia and other hon. gentlemen opposite will look at the export returns for the first nine or ten months of this year they will be happy, as we are happy, to see that there has been an increase in food exports. They will not, I am sure, be so happy to realize that that increase is not in our traditional markets. If my figures
Supp ly-A griculture
are correct, and I think they are, 70 per cent of that increase is with respect to communist countries and Cuba.
So that leaves a 30 per cent increase to the traditional markets.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. We are now in committee. I would ask all hon. members to cooperate so that the hon. member who has the floor may proceed. If any hon. gentleman has observations to make he may rise and do so when he is given the floor.

This increase is welcome, Mr. Chairman, because it reduces our surplus stocks of food, but one cannot help feeling anxiety arising from the fact that we cannot count on the continuation of exports to communist markets which have taken our goods because their people have been starving.
We on this side have complained, I think justifiably, that whereas, when we made an agreement with the Soviet union in regard to the export of food and other products all the details and the full terms of that agreement were made public and laid on the table of this house, we do not know even yet the terms of these agreements, letters of intent or contracts to which reference has been made. As I think this question is related to this item, it would be extremely helpful if the Acting Minister of Agriculture, before the debate on this item is concluded, would give us all the details of these contracts that have been made and which have resulted in the reduction of our surpluses and the increase of our wheat exports.
That has nothing to do with the item under consideration.
The acting minister does not want to hear it.
I will admit this has not very much to do with the item under consideration but I ask my hon. friend who brought up these matters?
The colleagues of the Leader of the Opposition raised these questions.

Perhaps I may conclude, Mr. Chairman, by repeating this one thought which did not seem to have made an impact on hon. gentlemen opposite when the hon. member for Essex East made the statement. We will support this item in the estimates as a measure of relief to farmers who deserve it. We deplore the fact that this kind of relief has to be given in this way through ad hoc items in the estimates brought in for a particular purpose at a time that seems most satisfactory to the government. We feel that this kind of thing should be based on principle and, when the time comes, we will bring in

Sup p ly-A gricu Iture
the type of legislation which will base it on principle and which will be much more satisfactory to our agricultural producers than anything the present government has done.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to direct a question to the Leader of the Opposition. Does the hon. gentleman agree with the basic principle expressed the other day by the hon. member for Burin-Burgeo which I took to be that we ought to be very careful, when we sell our wheat, that we do not also sell our freedom?

In answer to that question, Mr. Chairman, I would say this. We should be extremely careful to do nothing that would sell our freedom. We export for our own benefit primarily rather than exclusively for the benefit of the receiving country. With all respect to any other hon. member I do not think that in selling our wheat to countries which need our wheat we are selling our freedom.

Mr. Chairman, I had not planned to take part in this debate relating to an item of assistance to western grain producers in the amount of $42 million but after listening to apostle Paul and his ardent disciple from Assiniboia, last Friday and this evening respectively, I feel compelled to rise at this time. My determination to speak is given added weight as a result of the remarks we heard this evening from the lips of the Leader of the Opposition, the leader of this grand new party. After listening to his views on agriculture I feel it necessary to deal with some of the arguments that have been presented to the committee.
The matters raised by the hon. member for Essex East are easily answered. I propose to ignore them. After all, the hon. gentleman does not know anything about agriculture. As for the hon. member for Assiniboia, I shall deal with him a little later on.
It is small wonder that the Leader of the Opposition participated in this debate. He did so because the Liberal party is completely embarrassed by what the Conservative government has done for the Canadian people in the last four years.
I have before me some significant figures. During the last three years the Liberal government was in office it contributed to agriculture the total sum of $272,200,350. During the first three years the Conservative government has been in power it contributed to agriculture a total of $556,909,734.25. No wonder they are embarrassed. Hon. gentlemen opposite, to relieve their embarrassment and get themselves off the hook, are carping about a small item of $42 million being paid to western farmers.
The Leader of the Opposition indicated that the Liberals have a new agricultural policy which they will announce in due course. I hope the Leader of the Opposition will not take the advice of the Liberal party's adviser's Mr. Kent and Mr. Lamontagne, or we might have socialism in our farming industry.
The Leader of the Opposition spoke about P.F.A.A. The Liberals brought in P.F.A.A., he said. I will admit that the Liberals brought in P.FA..A. but the Liberals used the P.F.A.A. in western Canada to distribute Liberal propaganda. The Liberals were more interested in spreading propaganda than in assisting the farmers of western Canada. Let hon. gentlemen opposite rise and deny it. They cannot do so.
Let me relate a personal experience. Back in 1953 a by-election was held in our area. There was a Social Credit and a Liberal candidate. I supported the Liberal candidate because I did not want a Social Crediter sitting here doing nothing. They sat here for 17 years without accomplishing anything. After the election was over I was invited to the P.F.A.A. school. About 100 of us were in the room. The superintendent rose and said, "You fellows are all good Liberals or else you would not be here today. Go out to the farmers and do not take more than nine claims. And while you are doing that, preach Liberal politics to the farmers." That was the position of that Liberal with respect to P.F.A.A. Let hon. gentlemen opposite stand up and deny it. I challenge any hon. member opposite to deny it. They cannot do so.
They have the answers, all right.

When the Conservatives came into power the scope of P.F.A.A. was expanded. More farmers are receiving assistance today under this measure than ever was the case before. Approximately $60 million will be distributed to farmers this year under P.F.A.A.
We heard the hon. member for Assiniboia make reference to the march on Ottawa by the farmers. What was the hon. gentleman's attitude to the march on Ottawa? The C.C.F. hired a brass band which played "Happy Days are Here Again".
An article in the Winnipeg Free Press describes the actions of the C.C.F. in this respect. It states:
As delegates began to enter the station from the first train, C.C.F. members of parliament also outjockeyed the cabinet ministers for positions in what amounted to an informal receiving line.
C.C.F. House Leader Hazen Argue commented to a reporter, "It's all good clean fun".

That was the attitude of the hon. member for Assiniboia. He complained that the Prime Minister visited only northern Saskatchewan-
You are wrong again.

-and that the Minister of Agriculture visited only a large farm in Saskatchewan. However, I drove through southern Saskatchewan this summer and I found that grasshoppers were jumping all over the place. I said to the station agent, "You are not getting much of a crop this year". He said, "We are used to it. We never get a crop here. But if we had a decent government in Saskatchewan they woud rehabilitate that land and take care of it as was done in Alberta".
We have another statement of the hon, member for Assiniboia when the Minister of Agriculture was appointed. It is as follows:
The C.C.F. leader said he also is disappointed that the administration of the Canadian wheat board is to be dropped by the department of trade and commerce and to be taken over by the department of agriculture-
Mr. Argue posed the question: Will the department of trade and commerce give up its interest in selling the grain and further greatly weaken necessary export markets for wheat, oats and barley?
We do not need to say more about that. The Leader of the Opposition gets to his feet and says that the people are hungry. But this government sent men across the country to sell that wheat. Today we have cleaned up the surplus in western Canada. I felt sorry for one of the Liberal members here today who was called to order. I refer to the hon. member for Kent, New Brunswick. He rose in his place and pleaded for his little farmers in New Brunswick, and well he might do so. I went through that country three years ago. Many of those little farmers down there are destitute. Here we have a Liberal member who had to wait in order to get a Conservative government to do something for them. These people are going to get help from this government. We have a rehabilitation act coming into operation. It is a long term matter. These little farmers will be receiving help over the years not from a Liberal government but from a good Conservative government.
That is the Liberal answer, "Let the Conservatives do it".

We remember what started all the difficulties in western Canada.
The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate probably wants to start fishing or something now, I suppose.

If the hon. member would give me a chance to do so, I should like to talk about fish.
Supply-Agriculture

It would be nice to hear the hon. member talk about something he knows something about for a change. Back in 1946, when the Liberal government signed the wheat agreement, it cost the farmers in western Canada millions of dollars. What did our friend from Assiniboia say then? As reported in Hansard of August 15, 1946, at page 4839 the hon. member for Assiniboia said this:
I agree with the leader of this group (Mr. Coldwell) who stated that we in this party welcome the agreement.
A little farther on he said:
I welcome the wheat agreement.
He betrayed the farmers of western Canada. He sold them out. Now he comes to this House of Commons and wants us to subsidize them for what was done then.
We are only a little group.
We will ignore that remark.
Just a splinter group.

We know where it comes from. It is like getting kicked by a mule. Let us consider where it comes from and forget about it. Surely on an item like this, Mr. Chairman, we can stop this foolishness of trying to talk politics. Let us pass this item. It is what the farmers of western Canada need. They need acreage payments up to the 200 acre maximum. I am sure that every western member is in favour of it. I know they would like to see this legislation put on the statute books so that it is established on an annual basis for the farmers in lieu of the two-piece system. We get opposition every time we bring it in. The opposition parties want to make hay.
I do not wish to take up any more time, Mr. Chairman, and I thank you for the opportunity accorded to me to express my views.

It is always with humility, Mr. Chairman, that I rise to speak in this House of Commons, particularly when I follow the Leader of the Opposition and at a time when so many remarks have been made about an issue with which I wish to deal.
I should like to place on the record at this time the statement that I heartily support this motion. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I should like to put on the record some remarks that in my opinion have not been made as yet. The Leader of the Opposition is a man whom I respect greatly and whom I hesitate to follow and to criticize because I am a farmer. I farmed in the dirty thirties, in the dirty forties and in some of the fifties and I still am a farmer.

Supp ly-A griculture
There is one point that I think this committee and in fact the Canadian people should be reminded of. In speaking in support of this measure, one that is part of an over-all policy, I feel sincerely that there is one thing that should be put on the record. I have reference to some of the work behind the scenes. When I say that, what I mean is simply this. A few moments ago the Leader of the Opposition said that they counted on markets. Through you, Mr. Chairman, I should like to remind hon. members that this government has not counted on markets. They have done something about them. As I said before, the acreage payment is part of an over-all government policy. The thing that I should like to reiterate and put on record in reference to the agriculture economy of Canada is simply this. Much hard and sincere work has been done by this government. As a farmer I am proud to be here and to have an opportunity to speak in support of this measure.
You may recall, Mr. Chairman, when only a few short years ago-four or five years ago, as a matter of fact-in reference to wheat, our customers abroad in particular were giving us some trouble with regard to accepting purchases from Canada. When cargoes reached their destination there were often complaints and rejections for various reasons. When ships reached their destinations the cargoes did not measure up to the samples so far as quality was concerned. The reason for this was that cargoes were often contaminated by oil, coal dust or other foreign objects. The holds were not cleaned and in addition there were germs and insects in the cargoes. Something had to be done about it and the result was what we commonly call quality control.
You may think I am straying a little, Mr. Chairman, but this is all part of the same policy. I want to emphasize the work that has been done behind the scenes by the government. I should like to pay tribute to the former minister of agriculture because I know he did a great deal of work along this line. In fact, as a result of the work of the former minister we are assured now of satisfied customers almost universally. It was not easy to bring this about. Comparing the situation today with that prior to 1957-I need say no more as to dates-when our customers today receive a sample of our wheat and other export products as well, as a matter of fact they can rest assured that the cargo will be the same as the sample. Quality control is the answer.
What did this mean? It meant legislation and a great deal of work behind the scenes. As I said before, I should like to pay tribute

to the former minister of agriculture in this regard. I had not heard any reference to this point during this debate and there was very little I wished to say, but as far as I am concerned this is a great achievement because a satisfied customer is the best type of customer, particularly when he repeats his order. The reason why our customers are repeating their orders is that they can depend on the quality of Canadian products, not only agricultural products but every other product. The holds of ships have been thoroughly cleaned and for the first time our customers can be assured that the cargo will reach them in first class condition, whether the cargo be wheat, other types of grain or any other commodity. In other words, for the first time in history Canadian salesmen can go abroad and lay a sample on the table, and the customer can be assured that the product when delivered will be of the same quality as the sample. I think this fact should be recognized by hon. members opposite and the Canadian people generally and that is why I put it on the record.
With all deference and with great respect, as I said before, I should like to remind the Leader of the Opposition that we have not just counted on business but have been working for it. We have not counted on markets. I should like to join in complimenting the present Minister of Agriculture for the work he has done. Certainly no one can criticize his salesmanship. Unfortunately he is ill at the present time. This year we have sold 354 million bushels of wheat and flour and for this he should be commended to the utmost.
As a real farmer and having regard to parity of income I support to the utmost this measure making provision for acreage payments. Hon. members opposite can talk about business. I think I can talk about business as well. We all love election campaigns. I can recall that during the 1957 campaign certain people said, "You are a farmer, but what do you know about business"? All I could do was to remind them that any farmer who had his head above water financially at that time must have been a good businessman.
I rose with great humility to add my support to this measure and to remind hon. members and Canadians generally that such measures are not what they are said to be in certain quarters. This measure is part of an over-all policy. Actually it goes further than that. It represents co-operation among all segments of our nation because without the support of the eastern members the western members could not get very far. We appreciate the fact that all segments of the Canadian economy support this measure.

Finally, I should like to recall to hon. members the co-operation between the federal and provincial governments that has brought all this about. Certainly we can look forward in the very near future to much greater benefits from the policies of the present government.

Mr. Chairman, the item under consideration was not unexpected by western grain producers. The Prime Minister has compared it with the acreage payment made in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1959, and that made in the fiscal year ended March 31, 1961. I should like to quote from Hansard for August 30, 1958, page 4347. The Prime Minister was speaking and this is what he had to say:
-farm organizations over the years have contended that the Canadian consumer has been getting wheat too cheaply. Just as other producers expect a fair market price for their goods, so the Canadian wheat producer should receive a fair price for the wheat sold in the domestic market. That has been the general contention through the years.
Over a seven-year period the average domestic human consumption of wheat has been 45 million bushels. This is only 10 per cent of the total annual disposition of western wheat. An increase of 50 cents per bushel in the price of wheat for domestic consumption would be reflected in an increase of only 6.5 cents per bushel on the basis of total marketings. To achieve this would require a contribution to be made by parliament to the wheat board, or it would result in an estimated increase to the consumer of 2 cents per loaf of bread. Such a contribution would amount to a figure considerably lower than that which is proposed for this year only-
He went on to say:
This amount, which is designed to meet the needs of the small farmer, will be distributed by the Canadian wheat board to producers on the basis of one dollar per specified acre, including acreage seeded to flax, up to a maximum of 200 acres.
In the estimates for the period ending March 31, 1961, vote No. 576 of the supplementary estimates for that year, the payment was described as follows:
Payment of an amount, as a higher return for wheat used for human consumption in Canada, to western grain producers to be distributed on the following basis, namely: $1 per cultivated acre up to a maximum of 200 acres per farm in accordance with regulations of the governor in council.
The amount was $42 million, the same as it is today. The severe drought in some areas of the prairies is a matter of concern to all of us. It emphasizes the income problems in western Canada. However, acreage payments can hardly be considered crop failure payments. Members from western Canada have no intention of being drawn into that position by the opposition.
In order to deal with this matter effectively, it is necessary to recall the circumstances under which this party came into
Sup p ly-A griculture
office in 1957 and again in 1958. The situation in western Canada was desperate. During the preceding decade, a surplus of over 700 million bushels of wheat had been allowed to accumulate. Our country and terminal elevator systems were congested. Rigid quota regulations were necessary to ensure some equality of opportunity for delivery to country elevators. Elevator companies were forced into costly temporary and semi-permanent building programs in order to service a limited quota. Parliament found it necessary to establish the Temporary Wheat Reserves Act. The St. Laurent-Howe administration reduced the initial price for oats by five cents per bushel. This was another indication of the negative attitude that was developing at that particular time.
After the final settlement of the famous "have regard to" clause in the grain agreement with Great Britain, government policy drifted from one of selling to one of storing grain. During that period the bootleg trade of grain to feed mills, feeders and businessmen developed rapidly. This trend was accentuated by the failure of the St. Laurent-Howe government to adopt a policy of cash advances on farm stored grain. The sale of grain outside the Canadian wheat board was often completed allowing substantial discounts which were lost to the producer forever.
At that time, western Canada was represented in parliament by a strong opposition. The province of Alberta was represented almost entirely by Social Credit members led by their leader, Solon Low. The provinces of Manitoba and Saskatchewan sent large numbers of C.C.F. members led by their national leader, M. J. Coldwell, and strongly supported by Hazen Argue and Stanley Knowles. In addition to these members, the opposition could claim John Diefenbaker, Gordon Churchill and Douglas Harkness, all from the prairies. The government was represented by a numerical minority from the prairies. These Liberal members were led by the late Right Hon. James Gardiner and by Walter Tucker. There were some outstanding men among their numbers. Their impact on the large government majority from other parts of Canada was almost negligible. Indeed, the experience of my immediate predecessor in office on the question of cash advances revealed the extent to which party discipline had destroyed the effectiveness of parliamentary representation under the St. Laurent-Howe regime. The cash advance question was also vigorously advocated by the opposition, but without success.
After the election of 1957, the Diefenbaker administration effected a system of cash advances on farm stored grain. This relieved
3 42

Supply-Agriculture
some of the pressure on the farm cash position. It should be pointed out that cash advances were only an emergency measure. They became necessary only because of the continued failure of the St. Laurent-Howe government in its efforts to sell grain. The attitude of the Diefenbaker administration in 1957 and early 1958 encouraged the people in western Canada to reinforce his representation from the prairies. They did this despite the promises of Pearson and the Liberal party. They ignored the regional cry of the C.C.F., "Fight for the west.''
The Diefenbaker administration faced a mammoth task when it took office in 1958. The decay that had set in during the latter days of the 22 year tenure of Liberalism was widespread, and overlapped into almost every department of government. The Hon. Douglas Harkness was appointed minister of agriculture. It required almost two full years to effect the reorganization of the Department of Agriculture and to clear the way for legislation that might come to grips with the serious problems that required solution. The backlog of legislation requested by farm people was considerable and included farm credit arrangements, crop insurance, conservation, and the ordinary modernization of statutes already in effect, many of which had not been looked at since they were first placed on the statute books several years before.
It is small wonder, then, that farm people were impatient. They had waited a long time. The record of the previous Liberal government with regard to promises had been most frustrating. Thus it was that the "On to Ottawa" delegation was organized. The deficiency payments controversy was born. This government led by the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker, was not stampeded. This government made its decision.
The debates leading to that decision are a matter of public record. The record of the opposition groups cannot now be erased. The hon. member for Assiniboia chose to ignore the plea for a positive solution. He advocated an outright handout, a handout that would have aggravated our wheat surplus.
You are wrong again.
This handout would have encouraged the trend to larger farms and would have cost the treasury of Canada over a billion dollars.
Wrong again.

His attitude was clearly stated on April 23, 1959, as recorded at page 2973 of Hansard. I quote:
Western Canada today is being betrayed by members of parliament of the Conservative party who

represent them, in that they are opposed to the legitimate requests that have been made by the mass delegation.
In reply to that I said, as reported on the same page of Hansard:
No one has betrayed the western farmer more than those who during the years, not only this session but in past parliaments for the last 10 or 12 years, have taken stands in parliament that were so far from what the western Canadian farmer wanted that they engendered ill will from the other parts of this nation.
Silly talk.

The Liberal party, with its laissez faire outlook has consistently taken a negative stand on this matter. Their friends in Saskatchewan have been advocates of acreage reduction. The hon. member for Assiniboia, representing his party, has just as consistently advocated deficiency payments and he reiterated that stand on Friday last.
$100 million instead of $40 million.

The policy of the government has never been one of handouts. We refused to go back and pay for the short change policy of the former Liberal administration. Our ministers chose the positive approach in this matter.
The "On to Ottawa" delegation requested a payment of 31 cents per bushel for wheat in the year 1957-58, 12 cents for oats, and 23 cents for barley. I have their brief before me and also the prices for these grains in January, 1962, and the prices a year ago. No. 2 wheat is today $1.89 per bushel. Last year it was $1.62 and in March, 1959, it was $1.66. If we take the difference between 1959 and today, wheat is selling for 23 cents a bushel more than it did when the delegation came to Ottawa. No. 1 feed oats are selling at 90 cents a bushel today.
There is no crop.
Last year they sold at 70 cents a bushel-
You cannot sell what you have not got.

That price represents an increase of 20 cents per bushel. No. 1 feed barley is selling at $1.26 per bushel. Last year the price was 91 cents and in 1959 it was 99 cents. The difference between the price in March, 1959, and this year is 27 cents per bushel.
But there is no crop.
