In other words, the government's marketing, trade and fiscal policy has

resulted in achieving very closely the objectives requested by the "On to Ottawa" delegation.
But there were no crops.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order. The hon. member should be allowed to proceed without interruption, so that he may be heard.

I can understand the reason for the interruption because the hon. member does not like to hear of the achievements which this administration has been able to effect. The present vote proposes to continue the acreage payment for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1962, on the same basis as in 1960-61. Calculated on the basis of normal consumption in Canada, the returns on wheat used for human consumption are at or above the levels that farmers and farm organizations have maintained to be a parity price.
I can understand the consternation so evident among the members of the opposition. The hon. member for Assiniboia has called this acreage payment "peanuts", time and time again. However, he cannot defend that stand, particularly after renewing his old argument for deficiency payments. Without batting an eye he reversed his tactics and urged that this vote be made permanent and statutory. His conversion comes a little late; in fact, it comes four years too late.
On a point of order, Mr. Chairman, does the hon. member remember that in August, 1958, I asked that the legislation be made permanent?

You called it "peanuts" four years ago. You called it the same thing last year. When we first introduced acreage payments that was the time for the hon. member to give his support and endorsement of them.
That is what I did.

All we got at that time was a sneer and a snarl. The constituency of Assiniboia might just well have been represented in Timbuktu as in the House of Commons.
Liberal speakers have had a different purpose in their contributions. They have again been trying to divide Canada into east and west. The hon. member for Essex East used to impress us with his air of experience. All I can say is that he has learned little during the last four years except perhaps to stoop a little lower than he felt necessary when he was nearer his prime. That exhibition is becoming more pitiful with each passing day. Let us consider his reference to A.R.D.A., "that it is not designed to meet current situations". That is exactly the difference in attitude between the administration in which he was a leading
Supply-Agriculture
light and the administration of today led by the right hon. Prime Minister. They never planned for the future. They never moved except late and little. They blindly shut their eyes to the days when easy sales to Europe would come to an end as Europe recovered from starvation and the ravages of war.
The pledges made by the Prime Minister to the grain producers in western Canada have been fulfilled during the life of this parliament. The choice made by the people on the prairies in 1958 was a good one. Never before in Canadian history has their confidence been so influential here in Ottawa. Never before has the future held such promise for western grain producers. The Minister of Agriculture, the Hon. Alvin Hamilton, is one of the greatest living Canadians. His approach to farm problems and his sympathy for farm people have won him the respect and confidence of farm people from coast to coast.
What about his predecessor?

The Minister of Agriculture has been able to take farm problems to our urban neighbors and win their understanding and good will. This party and the people of the prairies are proud of him for the measures he has introduced to meet long range needs, and without which there can be no worthwhile future for people engaged in agriculture. All of us wish him a speedy return to the house and to the activity that he enjoys so much. It is hardly necessary for me to add that I support this measure.

I am glad to have the opportunity of participating in this debate because I have had so many requests for acreage payments during travels through my constituency. I told my constituents I was sure the government would not let them down.
I know I shall not be permitted to list the many sound pieces of legislation pertaining to agriculture introduced by the government under the great leadership of our Prime Minister, the Right Hon. John G. Diefenbaker. He is very highly respected and I can assure you that my constituents appreciate the co-operation we have had from the former minister of agriculture, the Hon. D. S. Harkness, and from our present Minister of Agriculture who is held in the greatest esteem throughout the dominion.
As all the western members with the exception of one from the three prairie provinces made strong representations seeking these acreage payments I was quite confident in telling my constituents that I was sure they would not be let down, particularly in a year such as this. As these representations favoured the two-price system they agreed that this

Supply-Agriculture
was the fairest way it would be paid. When one looks at how the acreage payments are made, he can easily see how the present government is trying to protect the family farms. The fact is that out of a total of 223,994 permit holders 179,951 are under 500 acres per permit, leaving only 44,043 over that amount.
The farmers in my constituency were very severely struck by drought, except in a few small areas. This made things very difficult that year, and this measure will certainly be greatly appreciated. Many farmers will be receiving the full benefit of prairie farm assistance. There are a great number just about on the line, who went over the 12 bushels, and I am sure that they, as well as those farmers who were under this amount, will very much appreciate these acreage payments.
I had the pleasure of having our Minister of Agriculture visit my constituency. I am more than happy with the wonderful job he did when we were faced with one of the worst drought conditions we have ever experienced. We very much appreciate the quick action taken by the minister and his department in alleviating the difficulties which might have led to a real panic on the livestock market. He took a great interest in the movement of grain and feed. The action of the minister and his department levelled the whole thing off and we did not run into any panic. Everything went along quite smoothly. I can assure hon. members that the farmers in my constituency, and all western farmers, very much appreciate what the government has done on their behalf.

Mr. Chairman, as a farmer in eastern Canada I should like to make a few remarks in connection with this legislation. First of all I wish to say that I am very much in favour of the acreage payment. I am very pleased to see it being brought forward at this time. I feel that the farmers in western Canada are very much entitled to some sort of assistance and this acreage payment will be very much appreciated by them.
I do not like to see it used as a subsidy to agriculture because I do not think it is such a subsidy. I should like this acreage payment to be placed on the basis of a direct subsidy to the consumer, a direct subsidy to the cost of living index, which is only one of the subsidies that those of us who are farming in other fields are helping to provide.
I think we all realize that the price of wheat on the export market is the selling price of grains in western Canada. We all

realize it is not the cost of production price that should be coming back to the farmers. It is based on a highly subsidized program from every country in the world and those of us in Canada, particularly the western farmers, have not been able to obtain a realistic price for grain.
We realize that there was a drought in western Canada and those of us in other parts of Canada think that anyone who loses a crop is entitled to some assistance. On the other hand, those of us from other parts of Canada are feeling the effects of that drought perhaps just as strongly as those who were affected in western Canada. Certainly the price of grains that we have to feed in the east has increased considerably, to the point where it is unprofitable for farmers in the east to feed these grains, having regard to the price of livestock. I hope the western farmer is getting the benefit of this increase in price that we have to pay.
To give hon. members some examples I obtained some prices the other day from some of our local mills. Sample wheat, with which hon. members from the west will be familiar-I think it is a sample 5 and 6 and some other grades mixed with it; it would be below No. 5 grade-is costing our retail outlets, with the freight assistance and subsidy taken off, $1.97 a bushel. Oats are today costing our own co-operative, with the freight subsidy removed, $1.09 a bushel. That is No. 1 feed oats. No. 1 barley is costing us $1.44 a bushel. The cost of the operation of the mill is about $6 a ton, which is added to that price before the farmer gets it on his farm to be fed. Hon. members will realize that if the farmer has to pay these prices for grains for his livestock he certainly is not in a position to make very much profit. I think this is the position with most of the farmers in Quebec and the maritimes.
Therefore I feel that if this policy is going to be a permanent one it should also be extended to other parts of Canada, because there are sections of eastern Canada which contain a great many farmers in the low income group. I hoped this policy would be made a two-price system because I think the man who is selling his wheat should receive a fair return for it. The subsidy would be placed in its rightful position. It might be a basis for subsidizing the low income farmers from other areas if this scheme were continued on an acreage payment basis and extended to other parts of Canada.
I think farmers in eastern Canada are very pleased if we see one section of the economy receiving some assistance, because

those in agriculture certainly need assistance regardless of where they are situated.
The minister of agriculture of Ontario, speaking at a farm meeting in Toronto a couple of weeks ago, suggested that the farmers of Ontario must grow their own grains. We cannot afford any more to buy grains and feed it to livestock at the prices we have to pay. The minister of agriculture in Ontario maintains that we have enough land in this province to do that.
I wonder what would happen if farmers in other parts of Canada did not buy western grains. We certainly appreciate what the Minister of Agriculture has done since he has been in office. We appreciate the amount of grain he has sold. This has certainly helped the west and it has helped those in the agricultural industry in all parts of Canada. It has helped those not only in the agricultural community but in every walk of life, because if the agricultural industry is down it affects the whole economy.
Business of the House
We realize that the minister has made some very good sales and this is reducing the surplus grain position in western Canada. I hope the minister will continue to make these contacts and these sales in other parts of the world.
Mr. Chairman, may I call it ten o'clock.
Progress reported.
